blurb: The machine learning that quietly runs the world: trees, clustering and the algorithms behind your feeds.

cards.title: Learning from tables

steps.p: Classic supervised learning starts with columns of features — age, price, clicks — and learns to predict a target.
Linear and logistic regression are fast, interpretable and still widely used.
Ensembles of decision trees, like random forests and gradient boosting, are often the strongest choice for spreadsheet-style data.

cards.aside: Fraud detection, credit scoring and demand forecasting still run largely on these methods.

cards.q: For typical tabular data, what often outperforms deep neural networks?
options: Gradient-boosted decision trees like XGBoost or LightGBM
cards.why: Gradient boosting. Benchmarks have repeatedly found tree ensembles match or beat deep nets on tabular data, while training faster and needing less tuning.

cards.statement: Logistic regression is used for classification, despite its name.
cards.why: True. It outputs a probability through the logistic (sigmoid) function, which is then thresholded into classes.

cards.q: A random forest makes predictions by…
options: Averaging many trees trained on random subsets of rows and features
cards.why: Averaging diverse trees. Each tree overfits differently; averaging cancels much of the noise. This is called bagging.

cards.title: XGBoost was used in 17 of the 29 winning Kaggle competition solutions published in 2015.
cards.detail: Tianqi Chen's gradient boosting library became the default tool for structured data competitions, according to the XGBoost paper.

cards.statement: Decision trees require features to be scaled to the same range.
cards.why: False. Trees split on thresholds of one feature at a time, so scale does not matter. Linear models and neural networks are the ones sensitive to it.

cards.title: Unsupervised learning

steps.p: Group similar examples together, such as customers with similar buying habits.
Compress many features into a few that keep the most important variation, for visualization or speed.
Learn what normal looks like and flag what doesn't fit, like fraudulent transactions.

cards.aside: No labels needed — the structure comes from the data itself.

cards.q: What must you choose before running k-means clustering?
cards.why: k. The algorithm assigns points to the nearest of k centers and moves the centers, repeating until stable. Choosing k is part of the art.

options: The directions along which the data varies most
cards.why: Directions of maximum variance. Projecting onto the top few components keeps most information in far fewer dimensions.

cards.statement: In a t-SNE plot, the distances between separate clusters are reliable.
cards.why: False. t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods but distorts global distances and cluster sizes. Two far-apart clusters may not be more different than two close ones.

cards.title: The k-means algorithm was developed at Bell Labs in 1957, but not published until 1982.
cards.detail: Stuart Lloyd described it in an internal report about signal processing. It is still one of the most widely used algorithms in data science.

cards.q: Which is a natural use for anomaly detection?
options: Flagging unusual credit card transactions as possible fraud
cards.why: Fraud. Fraud is rare and varied, so labeled examples are scarce. Modeling normal behavior and flagging deviations works well.

cards.title: "People like you also liked…"

steps.p: Find users with similar histories and recommend what they liked.
Learn a vector for every user and every item; their dot product predicts how much the user will like the item.
Large systems first narrow millions of items to hundreds of candidates, then a heavier model ranks those.

cards.aside: YouTube's widely read 2016 paper described this two-stage design.

cards.q: The "cold start" problem in recommendations refers to…
options: New users or items with no history to learn from
cards.why: No data yet. Collaborative filtering needs history. Systems fall back on content features, popularity or quick onboarding questions.

cards.q: The Netflix Prize offered $1 million for improving Netflix's rating predictions by…
cards.why: 10% in prediction error. The team BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos won in 2009, blending hundreds of models.

cards.statement: Netflix never deployed the full winning Netflix Prize solution.
cards.why: True. Netflix said the extra accuracy wasn't worth the engineering effort, and its business had shifted from DVDs to streaming.

cards.title: Matrix factorization became famous during the Netflix Prize.
cards.detail: Simon Funk publicly described a simple version in a 2006 blog post, and it quickly became a core technique of the competition and of recommender systems generally.

cards.q: In matrix factorization, a predicted rating is computed from…
options: The dot product of a learned user vector and a learned item vector
cards.why: A dot product. Dimensions often capture hidden tastes, such as how much a user likes action and how much action a film has.

cards.title: What your feed optimizes

steps.p: Modern feeds predict how likely you are to watch, like, share or comment, and rank by a weighted mix.
What you are shown shapes what you engage with, which shapes what you are shown next.
Optimizing immediate engagement can diverge from what users value over months.

cards.aside: This app's "Fewer" button is exactly the kind of explicit feedback engagement-driven feeds tend to underweight.

cards.q: Why can optimizing purely for watch time backfire?
options: It rewards compulsive content over content people value — a Goodhart's law problem
cards.why: Proxy vs goal. Watch time correlates with value until you optimize it hard; then it finds what is hardest to stop watching, not what is worth watching.

cards.statement: A recommender trained on clicks learns what users value in the long run.
cards.why: False. Clicks capture immediate impulses. Long-term satisfaction needs other signals, such as surveys, return visits or explicit feedback.

cards.q: Why do recommenders deliberately show some items they are unsure about?
options: Exploration — to learn about the user's tastes and avoid a narrow echo chamber
cards.why: Exploration. Without it, the system only ever confirms what it already believes about you.

cards.title: TikTok said in 2020 that whether you watch a long video to the end is a strong signal for its recommendations.
cards.detail: Its public explanation listed interactions, video information and device settings as factors, with completion among the strongest indicators of interest.

cards.title: Train your feeds on purpose
cards.body: Recommenders learn from every signal you give. Tapping "not interested" on a few items reshapes a feed faster than scrolling past them.
cards.challenge: On one app you use, mark three items "not interested" that you'd rather see less of.
